title: The ladder of humility (ch. 7)
hook: twelve steps, rising by going down

segments.voice: Yesterday, restraint of speech: even good words, held back sometimes, for silence's sake. Your line was fewer words. What filled the space you left? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

A ladder is about the simplest machine there is. Put your foot on the bottom rung, push, and you're higher. Up is up. Nobody has ever climbed a ladder by stepping down it. Chapter seven of Saint Benedict's Rule is built around a ladder. But this one works backward. On Benedict's ladder, the people who try to climb end up lower, and the ones who step down find themselves rising. Today's word is the name of that ladder.
screen: `UP IS UP.` → `A LADDER THAT WORKS BACKWARD.` → `STEP DOWN TO RISE.`

segments.voice: Benedict opens the chapter with Jesus's words in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted." Then he reaches back to Genesis, to Jacob asleep on a stone, dreaming of a ladder reaching to heaven with angels going up and down on it. Benedict reads the dream his own way. Going down, he says, is what happens when we lift ourselves up. Going up is what happens when we bend low. The ladder is our life. Its two side rails are body and soul. And between them God has set the rungs. Benedict counts twelve. The first is to keep the fear of God before your eyes and never forget it. Others you've already met this week: obedience is one rung, and holding back from too much talk is another. Some rungs are gentle: patience when things are hard, being content with the plain and the ordinary. Some are hard for a modern ear, like counting yourself lower than others, and readers today take those steps in different ways. The last rung is humility that shows in the body itself, in how a person walks and stands. And here's the surprise at the top. Benedict says that once all these steps are climbed, the monk arrives at the love of God that casts out fear, quoting the first letter of John: "perfect charity casteth out fear." The ladder starts with fear and ends with love. Humility, for Benedict, isn't thinking badly of yourself. It's getting out of your own way, until what's left is love, done easily, out of habit and delight.
screen: `WHO EXALTS HIMSELF SHALL BE HUMBLED.` · `JACOB'S LADDER, READ BACKWARD.` · `TWELVE RUNGS, FROM FEAR OF GOD UP.` · `AT THE TOP, LOVE THAT CASTS OUT FEAR.` · then, large: `PERFECT CHARITY CASTETH OUT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take a lower place. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the day ahead and look for one small seat you could take that's a step down. Letting someone else go first in line. Passing the credit for something to the person who helped. Taking the worse parking spot, the smaller slice, the end of the table. Pick one. Picture yourself doing it quietly, without anyone noticing that you chose it. Notice whether anything in you resists. Let it, and breathe out. If you pray, you can offer that small step down to God. The bell holds the time.
Humility. For Benedict, a ladder you rise on by stepping down, with twelve rungs and love at the top. Today's word.
Your line: down is up. Today, take the lower place once, on purpose and in secret, and see whether it feels like losing. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns hear chapter seven read in community, and some Catholics outside monasteries use its twelve steps as an examination of conscience.

fork.setup: you're Benedict, reading Jacob's dream of angels going up and down a ladder. what do you take it to mean?
options: the ladder shows how hard work gets you to heaven.
we go down by lifting ourselves up, and up by bending low.
the angels show that heaven is far away.
fork.reveal: Benedict reads it backward: we go down by exalting ourselves and go up by humbling ourselves.

The Rule is paraphrased. Check: ch. 7 opens with Luke 14:11; Jacob's ladder; 'we descend by exaltation and ascend by humility'; the ladder is our life, its sides body and soul; twelve degrees; first degree the fear of God kept always before the eyes; obedience (third degree) and restraint of speech (ninth through eleventh) among the steps; seventh degree (believing oneself lower than all) described as hard for modern readers; twelfth degree humility shown in bearing; the ending in the love that casts out fear, done as if naturally, from habit and delight in virtue.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Luke 14:11 and 1 John 4:18.
